The observed title page is arXiv:2608.06375v2 [cs.RO], dated 9 August 2026. The title and all eleven authors match the catalog. The catalog does not specify a revision; no earlier edition was supplied or compared.

All eleven supplied text chunks were individually read, covering all 39 PDF pages. The acquisition warning that text extraction does not reconstruct figure images was addressed by inspecting original PDF pages and six final crops. Figure 3 chart text was garbled in extraction and checked visually.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.

Visual inspection covers PDF pages 1–18, 22–27 and 33. Other task-gallery images were not visually inspected, although their complete supplied text was read. References were read without acquiring their cited works.
Code, external project resources and datasets were not inspected; no training or robot experiment was reproduced.

synopsis: ω-0 learns language-conditioned humanoid actions with auxiliary prediction of future visual latents. A pretrained action VLM and a joint query predictor condition a diffusion action head; SONIC executes its whole-body latents. Reported real-robot results favor this design, but camera differences, bundled ablations and inconsistent progress definitions limit causal interpretation.

problem.text: Wiping while stepping or carrying while turning requires coordinated legs, torso, arms and hands. The authors argue that separate locomotion/manipulation policies and video-centered action pipelines can impair this coordination. Their question is whether compact future representations can improve directly generated whole-body actions without decoding future videos for control.

contributions.text: A joint video-action latent predictor connects future visual supervision to controller-compatible action diffusion through motion-to-video cross-attention.
Staged learning transfers human visual-motion data through action-token pretraining and SONIC simulation replay, then adapts one policy to multiple real household tasks.
ω-HOME contains 40.3 hours, 4,827 episodes and 24 tasks at 30 Hz, with synchronized ego RGB, exo RGB-D, motion references, states and action latents.

inputs: Language instruction and a current view-tagged visual observation
Robot joint and hand positions plus IMU orientation represented in 6D; 47 state dimensions
outputs: Chunks of 66-dimensional actions: 64 SONIC latent coordinates and two scalar hand commands
Future Wan-space visual latents for predictive supervision and optional visualization

steps.name: Learn an action vocabulary
steps.detail: A whole-body FAST tokenizer reconstructs continuous trajectories with an L1 objective. Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct then predicts discrete action tokens autoregressively from language, an image and a view token; its hidden features become the later semantic prefix.

steps.name: Connect perception to future queries
steps.detail: Concatenate action-VLM features, T5 text features, a view token and frozen V-JEPA 2.1 image features. Prefix, motion and video tokens undergo separate self-attention; both query streams read the prefix, then motion queries read video queries. Visual-prefix, video and action tokens use 2D, 3D and temporal 1D RoPE respectively.

steps.name: Predict executable latents
steps.detail: Fuse future-aware motion features with text and encoded robot state. The 0.45B action DiT predicts clean action latents from noisy latents. A frozen Wan encoder supplies future visual targets; the optional Wan decoder is outside policy inference.

training.text: Stage 1 uses ARCTIC, Xperience-10M and Motion-X after conversion to unified SMPL. Stage 2 replays public motions through SONIC to obtain robot states and action latents, discarding untrackable or unsuitable motions. Filtering thresholds and retained subset sizes are unspecified.

Stages 2 and 3 freeze the action VLM, V-JEPA and Wan encoders while optimizing the joint predictor, state encoder, condition fusion and action DiT. Stage 2 combines clean-action prediction and future-latent squared error. Stage 3 uses 2,220 real trajectories across eleven tasks and replaces a random 0–8-frame noisy prefix with clean actions; loss applies only to the remaining actions.
All three stages use eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. This is training hardware, not a specified deployment benchmark configuration.

inference.text: Refresh the image and state, reuse the episode instruction, and sample actions with DDIM. Appendix B specifies H=25 predicted actions and K=8 executed before refreshing perception, an unexecuted previous segment as the next prefix, linear overlap blending, denormalization and SONIC execution. It reports approximately 0.14 seconds per forward pass, over 7 Hz inference; this does not establish the complete control-loop frequency.

Video decoding is explicitly unnecessary. Appendix B also calls the future-visual branch unnecessary for control, but does not explain how that statement relates to motion queries attending to video queries in the main formulation. Pruning the internal query pathway cannot be assumed.

equations.explanation: After prefix attention, motion queries q̄ᵐ read video queries q̄ᵛ as keys and values, producing motion features hᵐ. Video features hᵛ provide the predictive target interface; the direction is verified against Figure 2.

z₀ is the ground-truth action chunk, ẑ₀ the DiT prediction, and yᵛ the frozen Wan encoding of future observations. λvideo weights visual prediction. K here indexes the visual horizon; Appendix B separately reuses K for executed actions.
M is the clean prefix length and H the action horizon. Only the non-prefix actions receive denoising loss, while visual supervision remains active.

results.task: Eleven-task household loco-manipulation with egocentric input
results.setting: Real G1; one multi-task policy per method; ten trials per task; downstream humanoid demonstrations.
results.metric: Success rate; summed average subtask score /41; reported task progress
results.interpretation: Reported execution results, not video quality. The success advantage over ψ-0 is 34.6 percentage points (reader subtraction); baseline adaptations and progress ambiguity remain material.

results.task: Eleven-task household loco-manipulation with task-dependent viewpoints
results.setting: Omni uses exocentric inputs on five specified locomotion-heavy tasks and egocentric inputs on the remainder.
results.metric: Success rate; score /41; reported task progress
results.interpretation: The 2.7-point success gain changes inference viewpoint as well as training; it cannot establish an egocentric-only deployment benefit.

results.task: Removing future prediction and continuity components
results.setting: Table 4 real-world task-suite ablations; compare with full Ego.
results.metric: Success rate; score /41; reported task progress
results.interpretation: Video removal reduces success by 14.6 points, but jointly removes queries, the visual loss and motion-to-video attention. It does not isolate predictive supervision alone.

results.setting: Exclude eleven downstream tasks from the additional Stage-2 pool; then fine-tune on downstream training data.
results.metric: Success rate; score /41; reported task progress
results.interpretation: Reported gains are modest; uncertainty and denominators explaining these success percentages are not supplied.

results.task: Generalization across objects, scenes and human-data transfer
results.setting: Three object-variation tasks, two scene-variation tasks, and one human-trained closet-closing task; object/scene models fine-tuned on full ω-HOME.
results.metric: Success rate; score; reported task progress
results.value: With video queries: objects 83.3%, 11.8/13, 90.8%; scenes 79.5%, 5.5/6, 91.7%; human transfer 60.0%, 2.2/3, 74.6%.
results.interpretation: These are adapted-policy evaluations. Trial denominators and uncertainty are unclear, especially for the reported 79.5% over two scene tasks; this is not broad zero-shot task generalization.

limitations.text: The main definition assigns progress m/n when the first failure occurs at subtask m, while Appendix E describes completed-stage fractions. Table 8 contains later successes after earlier failures, so the conventions differ. Treat progress as a reported, unresolved metric rather than an unambiguous measure of uninterrupted execution.

Baseline action interfaces, backbones and chunking differ; GR00T uses sequential chunks without the same RTC. Shared downstream evaluation does not isolate world modeling from controller compatibility, capacity or training priors.

Figure 5 is a radar plot although its caption describes rollout sequences. Table 1 names fridge drink retrieval, while Table 16 and Figure 22 specify apple-and-pomegranate retrieval. These internal presentation differences remain unresolved.

The source reports no confidence intervals or repeated-training-seed uncertainty. Human-transfer evidence covers one specified task, and SONIC filtering restricts the motion distribution. The paper has no dedicated limitations section.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the pretrained encoders/VLM, SONIC-compatible labels and controller, and synchronized robot data. Appendix A specifies 66 action and 47 state dimensions, mean/standard-deviation normalization for the 64 body latents, min-max scaling for states/hands, z-up coordinates and initial-yaw subtraction.

Missing essentials include exact public-data filters and split manifests, optimization schedules, λvideo, DDIM step count, overlap length and deployment hardware. Appendix B's prose places stitching before execution, but Algorithm 1 lists execution before blending; scheduling and whether prefixes are clamped throughout denoising need clarification.

reasoning.text: The WAM and latent-prediction labels fit. The recorded IDM/Q4 label does not: the source explicitly rejects test-time video-to-action inversion and directly denoises actions conditioned on learned future-aware queries. The predictor and action DiT are distinct modules, so their joint loss also cannot establish a single shared-backbone One Model architecture. This is an assessment of the unchanged catalog snapshot, not a replacement classification.

discussionQuestions: Does aligned future supervision help when query capacity and attention topology are held fixed?
Which internal video-query computations remain active at deployment, and how is progress computed from non-prefix trial annotations?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title/author block and arXiv margin stamp
evidence.detail: Observed title exactly matches the supplied primary title. Authors are Zhe Li, Zhenzhe Zhang, Yangyang Wei, Wenjie Zhang, Xichen Yuan, Peiyuan Zhi, Gen Li, Xinying Guo, Fengjie Gao, Jianfei Yang and Shanghang Zhang. The stamp is arXiv:2608.06375v2 [cs.RO], 9 Aug 2026; affiliations are MARS Lab, NTU; PKU; BAAI; HKUST(GZ).

evidence.location: PDF pp. 2–3, Section 1, motivation and contributions
evidence.detail: Concurrent loco-manipulation motivates learning whole-body coordination and compact predictive visual supervision rather than a video-centered action pipeline.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 5, Figure 2 and caption
evidence.detail: The architecture has an action VLM, joint latent predictor and 0.45B action DiT, with SONIC execution. Figure 2 directs future action features into condition fusion; its Wan decoder visualizes future latents.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, tokenizer and autoregressive-loss equations
evidence.detail: FAST encodes action chunks, reconstructs them with L1 loss, and supplies discrete labels for Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct next-token training. Hidden VLM features are reused in subsequent stages.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.3, prefix construction, RoPE and final attention equations; p. 5, Figure 2 right panel
evidence.detail: Current features come from V-JEPA 2.1; T5, a view token and action-VLM features form the prefix. Motion/video queries separately read the prefix before motion queries attend to video queries. Spatial RoPE excludes text, view and VLM summary tokens.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 3.3, visual loss, condition fusion, x0 objective and frozen-module paragraphs
evidence.detail: Wan future latents supervise squared error. The DiT predicts clean actions and uses DDIM at inference. V-JEPA, Wan and the VLM remain frozen. Video decoding is optional and outside real-time policy inference.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 3.4, RTC equations; p. 8, Section 3.5; p. 16, Section 6.5, Training-time RTC
evidence.detail: Fine-tuning replaces a clean action prefix and scores only the remaining actions. The ablation discussion specifies random prefix lengths between 0 and 8. Deployment reuses preceding predictions for continuity.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–9, Sections 4–4.3 and Figures 3–4; p. 10, Section 5.1
evidence.detail: ω-HOME reports 40.3 hours, 4,827 episodes, 24 tasks and 30 Hz multimodal recordings. Teleoperation uses Pico devices, ZED cameras and Inspire hands. Public training sources are ARCTIC, Xperience-10M and Motion-X; unsuitable motions are filtered before controller-supervised learning. Downstream fine-tuning uses 2,220 trajectories across eleven tasks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 22, Appendix A.1–A.3, action/state definitions and normalization equations
evidence.detail: Actions have 64 controller latent dimensions plus two bounded hand commands; state has 47 dimensions and excludes IMU acceleration/angular velocity. The appendix specifies 6D orientation, separate normalization, SMPL conversion, z-up coordinates and zero-yaw preprocessing.

evidence.location: PDF p. 23, Appendix B.1–B.2, overlap equation and Algorithm 1 lines 4–12
evidence.detail: A forward pass is approximately 0.14 s; H=25 and K=8. Unexecuted actions warm-start the next chunk; overlaps are linearly blended and latents denormalized. The prose says stitching precedes sending actions, whereas Algorithm 1 lists execution at line 10 and blending at line 12. The future-visual branch is described as unnecessary for real-time control.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–12, Sections 6.1–6.4 and Table 1; p. 17, Section 6.6
evidence.detail: The main evaluation uses one multi-task model per method and ten trials per task. Success requires all objectives; score counts completed subtasks. Baselines use adapted action heads and differing chunking/control interfaces. Section 6.6 states that G1 evaluation rollouts are autonomous, without teleoperation, replay or scripted intervention.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Table 2, ω-0 Ego, ω-0 Omni, ψ-0 and DiT4DiT rows, all metric columns
evidence.detail: Table 2 reports Ego 79.1/35.8/88.7, Omni 81.8/36.7/90.3, ψ-0 44.5/23.6/59.6 and DiT4DiT 43.6/23.1/61.0 for success percent, score out of 41 and progress percent. No uncertainty is shown.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 13–14, Section 6.4, Ego/Omni viewpoint paragraphs
evidence.detail: Ego uses egocentric observations for training and evaluation. Omni uses exocentric observations on clothes-to-basket, towel-to-washer, mopping, garbage collection and apple/drawer tasks; remaining tasks use egocentric observations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Table 3, all rows; p. 14, Section 6.4, additional ω-HOME data paragraph
evidence.detail: Adding non-overlapping ω-HOME tasks to Stage 2 changes Ego SR/score/progress from 79.1/35.8/88.7 to 80.4/36.9/89.7 and Omni from 81.8/36.7/90.3 to 82.4/37.5/91.2. Downstream tasks are excluded from the additional pretraining pool.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, Table 4, all rows; pp. 15–16, Section 6.5
evidence.detail: Success rates are 60.9 without state, 66.4 without VLM prefix, 64.5 without video queries, 71.8 without RTC and 63.6 with Wan as current encoder, versus Ego 79.1 and Omni 81.8. Video ablation removes queries, visual loss and motion-to-video attention together. Better offline Wan latent reconstruction is discussed qualitatively, without a numerical reconstruction table.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Section 6.7, setting definitions and ablation; p. 18, Table 5 and score-maxima caption
evidence.detail: Three object tasks, two scene tasks and one human-transfer task are described. Table 5 with/without-query SR is 83.3/66.7, 79.5/15.0 and 60.0/20.0 respectively; scores and progress are reported for each setting, with maxima 13, 6 and 3. Exact trial denominators and uncertainty are not given here.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Section 6.1, Task Progress paragraph; p. 26, Appendix E.2; p. 27, Figure 10 caption
evidence.detail: The main text defines progress from the first failing subtask m as m/n. Appendix E.2 and Figure 10 instead describe a normalized fraction of completed stages. These definitions are not equivalent for later successes following earlier failures.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 24–25, Appendix C.1–C.2, Tables 6–16; specifically p. 24, Table 8 all rows and trials
evidence.detail: Binary annotations mark completed physical milestones. In Table 8, Trial 1 is 1,0,1,0,0 and Trial 2 is 1,0,1,1,0, demonstrating non-prefix completion. All-five-stage columns occur in Trials 4 and 7–10.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Figure 5 panels, legend and caption
evidence.detail: The visual is three radar plots for score, success and progress. Its caption instead describes task instructions and orange markers over robot rollout sequences; the caption and graphic do not match.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Table 1 row 11; p. 25, Table 16; p. 33, Figure 22 task card
evidence.detail: The main task list labels fridge drink retrieval, whereas detailed annotations and the task card describe retrieving apple and pomegranate into a basket and closing the fridge.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Section 6 Implementation Details; p. 23, Appendix B.1
evidence.detail: Training uses eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The latency paragraph reports forward-pass time without specifying deployment hardware or full end-to-end control timing.
